title: Clinical Trials
description: Clinical trial costs can qualify for the federal R&D credit under IRC Section 41 when trials resolve technical uncertainty through experimentation.

body.text: Clinical trial costs can qualify for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41 when trials resolve technical uncertainty through a process of experimentation. For U.S. drug, biologic, and device sponsors, IRS guidance generally does not challenge Phase I and II expenses, while Phase III and IV costs require detailed documentation of unresolved uncertainties.
Executive Summary

Clinical trials constitute the most capital-intensive and scientifically rigorous phase of therapeutic development in the biopharmaceutical and medical device industries. Within the United States federal income tax system, expenditures incurred to design, execute, and analyze clinical trials are evaluated for tax credit eligibility under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41), titled the Credit for Increasing Research Activities and commonly referred to as the Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit. Because the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) mandates structured human clinical testing prior to granting marketing approval for novel drugs and therapeutic biologics, clinical trial protocols inherently operate as systematic, hypothesis-driven investigations designed to resolve biological, pharmacological, and methodological uncertainties. Consequently, clinical development activities frequently qualify as Qualified Research Activities (QRAs), generating Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) that offset federal tax liabilities dollar-for-dollar.

The substantive evaluation of clinical trial expenditures under IRC § 41 hinges on the progressive resolution of technical uncertainty across the four phases of clinical development. Under administrative guidance issued by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) for the pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries, examiners are instructed generally not to challenge QREs incurred during Phase I and Phase II clinical trials, establishing an administrative non-challenge zone grounded in the high degree of scientific uncertainty governing early-stage human safety, dosing, and efficacy. Conversely, expenditures incurred during large-scale Phase III confirmatory trials and post-marketing Phase IV studies fall outside this general non-challenge directive—save for specific confirmatory trials mandated by the FDA under Accelerated Approval pathways—and require granular documentation demonstrating that the activities resolve novel technical uncertainties rather than executing routine quality control or post-production verification.
Regulatory Mandate and Fiscal Significance of Clinical Trials
Scientific Progression and Regulatory Mandate of Clinical Trial Phases

Clinical trials are prospective biomedical or behavioral research studies conducted in human participants to evaluate the safety, dosage, pharmacokinetics, and clinical efficacy of investigational interventions, including small-molecule drugs, medical devices, and therapeutic biologics such as vaccines or gene therapies. Under FDA regulatory mandates, sponsors may initiate human clinical testing via an Investigational New Drug (IND) application only after pre-clinical laboratory and animal toxicity studies demonstrate an acceptable initial safety profile. Human clinical investigation then proceeds through four sequential, progressively scaled phases that systematically address distinct scientific unknowns.

Phase I clinical trials represent the initial introduction of an investigational candidate into human subjects, typically enrolling approximately 20 to 80 participants to evaluate acute safety, determine a safe dosage range, identify side effects, and characterize pharmacokinetics—specifically how the investigational compound is absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and excreted in vivo. Once initial human safety and pharmacokinetic parameters are established, Phase II clinical trials expand enrollment to approximately 100 to 300 patients diagnosed with the target disease or condition. The primary scientific objectives in Phase II are to evaluate preliminary clinical efficacy (effectiveness), further assess short-term safety and adverse events, and refine the optimal dosing schedule and delivery methodology. The standard FDA and National Institutes of Health (NIH) baseline ranges are 20 to 80 participants for Phase I and 100 to 300 patients for Phase II, establishing a standard combined boundary of 20 to 300 participants, although complex adaptive Phase IIb protocols occasionally extend enrollment up to 500 patients.

Following successful Phase II studies, Phase III clinical trials represent the most resource-intensive stage of clinical development, enrolling several hundred to several thousand (typically 300 to 3,000 or more) patients across diverse demographic and clinical subpopulations. These large-scale, often randomized and double-blinded trials confirm clinical effectiveness, compare the investigational therapy against current standard-of-care treatments or placebos, detect less common adverse reactions, and establish the comprehensive risk-benefit profile required for FDA marketing approval via a New Drug Application (NDA) or Biologics License Application (BLA). Finally, Phase IV clinical trials are conducted during the post-approval stage after the FDA grants commercial marketing authorization, encompassing post-marketing surveillance, long-term safety monitoring, pharmacovigilance, and real-world effectiveness evaluations across the broader patient population. For tax policy purposes under IRC § 41, this FDA-mandated progression provides the objective structural scaffolding required to demonstrate a statutory "process of experimentation," as the clinical protocol functions as the controlled empirical mechanism through which a sponsor tests hypotheses and resolves biological uncertainty.
Capital Intensity and the Interplay Among IRC Section 41, IRC Section 174, IRC Section 174A, and IRC Section 45C

The biopharmaceutical R&D lifecycle is characterized by prolonged development timelines, substantial capital outlays, and high clinical attrition rates. The R&D Tax Credit under IRC § 41—which was permanently extended by Section 121(a) of the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (Pub. L. 114-113, Division Q, enacted December 18, 2015) for amounts paid or incurred after December 31, 2014—serves as a critical fiscal mechanism to reduce the after-tax cost of clinical experimentation. By generating a direct dollar-for-dollar reduction in federal income tax liability (or, for eligible qualified small businesses under IRC § 41(h), a payroll tax credit election of up to $500,000 per year against employer Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes under IRC § 3111 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022) based on qualifying clinical trial expenditures, the IRC § 41 credit preserves operating liquidity that life sciences enterprises can redeploy into high-risk pipeline programs.

For clinical-stage companies developing therapeutics targeting rare diseases or conditions (orphan drugs), the IRC § 41 research credit operates alongside the Orphan Drug Tax Credit codified under IRC § 45C. Under IRC § 45C(a), a taxpayer may elect to claim a tax credit equal to 25% of its "qualified clinical testing expenses" paid or incurred during the taxable year (reduced from 50% to 25% under the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act). To prevent double-counting of identical clinical trial outlays, the statutory coordination rules of IRC § 45C(c)(1) mandate that any qualified clinical testing expenses taken into account in computing the 25% Orphan Drug Credit under IRC § 45C cannot be included in current-year QREs for purposes of calculating the IRC § 41 research credit. However, as confirmed by the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit in United Therapeutics Corp. v. Commissioner, No. 23-1718 (4th Cir. June 24, 2024), aff'g 160 T.C. (2023) (2023 WL 3496208), IRC § 45C(c)(2) strictly requires taxpayers to include those overlapping qualified clinical testing expenses (to the extent they also meet the definition of QREs under IRC § 41(b)) when calculating their historical "base period research expenses"—including the three-year rolling average QRE base under the Alternative Simplified Credit—when applying IRC § 41 to subsequent taxable years.

Furthermore, evaluating the cash-flow mechanics of clinical trial tax incentives requires distinguishing between two statutory eras governing the deductibility of research and experimental (R&E) expenditures: the 2022–2024 mandatory capitalization period enacted under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206) and the post-2024 domestic expensing regime enacted under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21, Title VII, § 70302, signed July 4, 2025).

Under the TCJA amendments to IRC § 174, which governed taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, Congress eliminated the historical option to immediately deduct R&E expenditures in the year incurred. During the 2022 through 2024 taxable years, taxpayers were required to capitalize specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures and amortize them ratably over a five-year period for domestic research (or a 15-year period for foreign research), beginning at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenses were paid or incurred, which allowed only a 10% deduction for domestic clinical trial costs in the first year. Because mandatory five-year capitalization under TCJA § 174 deferred 90% of first-year tax deductions and increased near-term taxable income for clinical-stage companies, the immediate tax liability offset provided by the IRC § 41 credit directly mitigated the resulting liquidity compression.

On July 4, 2025, Section 70302 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21, 139 Stat. 72, 192–193) fundamentally reshaped this framework by adding IRC § 174A (Domestic research or experimental expenditures, 26 U.S.C. § 174A) and narrowing IRC § 174 exclusively to foreign research. Under IRC § 174A(a), for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, taxpayers are once again permitted to immediately deduct 100% of domestic research or experimental expenditures—including U.S. clinical trial costs and software development under IRC § 174A(d)(3)—in the taxable year paid or incurred. Alternatively, under IRC § 174A(c), a taxpayer may elect to capitalize and amortize domestic R&E expenditures ratably over a period of not less than 60 months.

In contrast, OBBBA § 70302(b)(1) retained mandatory capitalization and 15-year (180-month, mid-year convention) amortization under amended IRC § 174 for all foreign research or experimental expenditures, such as clinical trial operations conducted outside the United States. Moreover, under OBBBA § 70302(b)(1)(C)(ii) amending IRC § 174(d), if property related to foreign R&E expenditures is disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025, no immediate deduction or reduction to amount realized is permitted on account of that disposition; the taxpayer must continue amortizing those foreign research costs over the remainder of the original 15-year schedule.

To transition from the 2022–2024 TCJA capitalization regime to IRC § 174A, OBBBA § 70302(f) and IRS Revenue Procedures 2025-23, 2025-28, and 2026-32 (released September 4, 2026, expanding automatic change relief through taxable years beginning before January 1, 2028) establish targeted recovery procedures. Taxpayers with unamortized domestic R&E balances capitalized during 2022 through 2024 may elect an automatic change in method of accounting (using Designated Change Number [DCN] 273 for IRC § 174A changes and transition methods, alongside DCN 265 for TCJA § 174 changes and DCN 274 for foreign expenditures) to deduct the remaining unamortized domestic balance either in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over a two-year period (2025 and 2026 for calendar-year taxpayers). Additionally, eligible small businesses meeting the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test ($31 million or less in three-year average annual gross receipts) were granted a one-time window under OBBBA § 70302(f)(1) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 to retroactively apply IRC § 174A to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 (and to make a late election or revoke a prior election under IRC § 280C(c)(2)) on amended returns; however, that statutory election window closed on July 6, 2026.
Statutory Framework: Applying the IRC Section 41(d) Four-Part Test to Clinical Experimentation

To qualify for the R&D tax credit, clinical trial activities must satisfy the statutory Four-Part Test codified in IRC § 41(d)(1) and elaborated in Treasury Regulations 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4. Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A), this four-part test must be applied separately with respect to each discrete "business component" of the taxpayer. In the life sciences sector, the business component—defined under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer—is typically the candidate drug formulation, therapeutic biologic, medical device, or associated manufacturing and clinical delivery process. Under the "shrinking-back rule" of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), if the requirements of IRC § 41(d) are not met at the level of the discrete business component as a whole, they are applied to the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention, continuing down until either a subset of elements that satisfies the requirements is reached or the most basic element fails to satisfy the test.

headers: Clinical Trial Application and Substantiation Focus

cells: Activity must intend to develop a new or improved business component relating to function, performance, reliability, or quality (excluding style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design).

Investigating a novel therapeutic mechanism to treat an unmet medical need (new function) or achieving superior clinical efficacy, bioavailability, or reduced toxicity over existing standards of care (improved performance, safety, or quality).
Information sought to be discovered must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

Protocols rely directly on molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, pharmacology, immunology, human physiology, and biostatistics to measure pharmacodynamic responses, biomarker endpoints, and adverse event profiles.

Expenditures must qualify as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A (or § 174 for pre-2025 years) undertaken to discover information intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design of the business component.

Pre-clinical animal models cannot establish human systemic behavior; uncertainty exists regarding whether the therapeutic will achieve target efficacy safely in humans (capability), via what dosing schedule or delivery route (method), and under what protocol and stratification parameters (appropriate design).
Substantially all (≥80%) of the research activities must constitute elements of a systematic process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to resolve the technical uncertainty.

Hypothesis formulation, iterative dose escalation (e.g., 3+3 oncology designs), adaptive trial arms, comparative biomarker validation, patient-stratification algorithms, and protocol amendments driven by emerging clinical data.

body.text: Criterion 1: Permitted Purpose (Function, Performance, Reliability, or Quality)

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)(A), as detailed in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), research is conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component. Clinical trials conducted to develop novel pharmaceuticals or biologics inherently satisfy this requirement because the investigation seeks either to establish a new therapeutic function—treating a pathology for which no adequate therapy exists—or to achieve measurably improved clinical performance through higher response rates, improved pharmacokinetic stability, lower toxicity, or enhanced patient tolerability compared to existing standards of care. Conversely, IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii) explicitly disqualify research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors, requiring sponsors to ensure that purely aesthetic formulation modifications are segregated unless directly tied to functional bioavailability or pediatric compliance metrics.
Criterion 2: Technological in Nature

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), the activity must seek to discover information that is technological in nature, meaning the process of experimentation used to discover such information fundamentally relies on the principles of the hard sciences: physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and (a)(4), a taxpayer may employ existing technologies and rely on existing principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science to satisfy this requirement, and does not need to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field or succeed in developing the new or improved business component. Clinical trials systematically apply the scientific method across pharmacology, biochemistry, human physiology, pathology, and biostatistics. The quantitative measurement of pharmacokinetic parameters, pharmacodynamic biomarkers, dose-response curves, and statistical efficacy endpoints under FDA-regulated protocols confirms a direct reliance on biological and physical sciences, distinguishing clinical trials from social science, market research, or consumer preference studies excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and (G).
Criterion 3: Elimination of Technical Uncertainty (The Section 174A / Section 174 Test)

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)—as amended by Section 70302 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024—qualified research must be research "with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A" (and for taxable years prior to 2025, under IRC § 174 as elaborated in Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i)). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer as of the outset of the research does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component.

In clinical development, technical uncertainty is the foundational reason the FDA requires human trials prior to commercialization. Pre-clinical in vitro assays and in vivo animal models provide only preliminary indications of biological activity and cannot establish complex human immunology, metabolism, or systemic toxicity. First, capability uncertainty exists because the sponsor does not know at the outset whether the candidate molecule or biologic can safely achieve the intended therapeutic efficacy in a live, heterogeneous human biological system without inducing unacceptable dose-limiting toxicities. Second, method uncertainty persists regarding the specific administration route, formulation matrix, delivery mechanism, or dosing regimen required to maintain therapeutic systemic exposure. Third, appropriate design uncertainty governs the optimal clinical trial protocol architecture, inclusion and exclusion patient stratification criteria, dosage titration rules, and surrogate or clinical biomarker endpoints needed to isolate and validate treatment effects. Notably, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) confirms that a taxpayer may undertake a qualifying process of experimentation even if there is no uncertainty concerning capability or method, so long as the appropriate design of the desired result is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities.

Crucially, the magnitude of technical uncertainty is not static across the clinical lifecycle; rather, it diminishes as empirical data accumulate across successive phases. While fundamental uncertainty regarding human safety and efficacy dominates Phases I and II, by the time a compound enters Phase III, primary capability and dosing method uncertainties may already be substantially narrowed. Consequently, sustaining QRE eligibility in Phase III requires demonstrating that specific, unresolved technical uncertainties persist—such as unexpected subpopulation metabolic variances, drug-drug interactions, immunogenicity in broader cohorts, or adaptive protocol redesigns triggered by interim safety signals.
Criterion 4: Process of Experimentation and the 80% Substantially All Rule

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), the taxpayer must engage in a process of experimentation designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) specifies that a process of experimentation must fundamentally rely on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science and involves three core elements: (1) the identification of uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component; (2) the identification of one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty; and (3) the identification and conduct of a process of evaluating the alternatives (through, for example, modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology).

Furthermore, under the "substantially all" rule of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), at least 80% (≥80%) of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component, measured on a cost or another consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to the employee-level 80% rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)), must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose described in IRC § 41(d)(3). If 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, the "substantially all" requirement is satisfied even if the remaining 20% or less of research activities do not constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, so long as those remaining research activities satisfy the requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and are not otherwise excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4).

Clinical trials satisfy this requirement through their structured, iterative evaluation of scientific hypotheses. Qualifying experimental activities include designing and validating novel clinical protocols (such as adaptive trial arms, dose-escalation matrices like the 3+3 oncology design, or decentralized clinical trial models), developing proprietary patient-stratification algorithms or predictive retention models, comparing alternative dosing cohorts or companion diagnostic biomarkers side-by-side, and executing formal protocol amendments in response to interim adverse event or efficacy data. However, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(7), the employment of computers or information technology to store, collect, manipulate, translate, disseminate, produce, distribute, or process data or information does not by itself establish that qualified research has been undertaken.
Regulatory Nexus: IRS Administrative Guidance and Audit Risk Allocation by Trial Phase

This administrative framework segments pharmaceutical and biologic development into four distinct stages: Stage 1 (Pre-Clinical/Discovery Research), Stage 2 (Clinical Trial Stage, encompassing Phases I, II, and III), Stage 3 (Regulatory Review), and Stage 4 (Post-Approval Stage, encompassing Phase IV trials).
The IRS Administrative Directive and the Phase I/II Non-Challenge Zone

Under the IRS pharmaceutical industry directive, examiners are instructed that they should generally not challenge the amount of QREs claimed by a taxpayer to the extent those expenditures are incurred for qualified research activities occurring during Stage 1 (Discovery/Pre-Clinical) and Phase I and Phase II of Stage 2 (the Clinical Trial Stage), provided the taxpayer maintains adequate substantiation verifying that the expenses were actually incurred and properly allocated.

This administrative posture functions as a de facto compliance safe harbor for early-stage clinical trials. The regulatory rationale rests on the recognition that Phase I trials—establishing initial human safety, tolerability, dose range, and pharmacokinetics—and Phase II trials—determining preliminary clinical efficacy and refining dosing regimens in affected patient cohorts—are overwhelmingly governed by fundamental scientific uncertainty. Because the compound's biological capability and method of administration in humans remain unproven during Phases I and II, the clinical trial activities inherently constitute a statutory process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C).
Audit Risk Allocation and Statutory Exclusions in Phase III and Phase IV Trials

In contrast to the administrative protection afforded to Phases I and II, activities conducted during Phase III of Stage 2 and throughout Stage 4 (the Post-Approval Stage, including Phase IV clinical trials) are explicitly excluded from the IRS general non-challenge directive, with a narrow regulatory carve-out for specific confirmatory trials required by the FDA under Accelerated Approval regulations (21 C.F.R. Part 314 Subpart H for drugs and 21 C.F.R. Part 601 Subpart E for biologics).

This structural divergence creates an inverse relationship between financial expenditure volume and automatic audit protection. During an IRS examination of Phase III or Phase IV claims, auditors evaluate whether core uncertainties regarding the drug's capability and therapeutic method were already resolved at the conclusion of Phase II, potentially triggering statutory exclusions under IRC § 41(d)(4) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c).

The first major statutory hazard is the exclusion for research after commercial production under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), which disqualifies any research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component. Under IRS examination guidelines and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c), a business component is considered ready for commercial production when it is developed to the point where it is ready for use or meets the basic functional and economic requirements of the taxpayer, and activities such as preproduction planning for a finished business component, tooling up for production, trial production runs, and accumulating data relating to production processes are deemed to occur after commercial production begins. While Phase IV trials occur after FDA marketing approval and commercial launch—rendering them presumptively ineligible unless conducted to resolve novel technical uncertainties for a new indication, a new formulation, or a mandatory FDA Accelerated Approval confirmatory endpoint—Phase III trials can also attract scrutiny under this exclusion if costs are incurred close to or overlapping with commercial manufacturing scale-up and NDA or BLA filing.

The second major statutory hazard is the routine testing, quality control, and routine data collection exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c), which disqualifies efficiency surveys, management functions or techniques, market research or development (including advertising or promotions), routine data collection (IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(iv)), and routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control (IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(v)). If a Phase III study merely executes large-scale confirmatory data collection to satisfy regulatory sample-size requirements without evaluating uncertain technical parameters, IRS examiners may reclassify the expenditures as non-qualifying verification or routine data collection. Similarly, examiners screen clinical activities against the adaptation exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and duplication exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(C). To substantiate Phase III QREs under examination, life sciences taxpayers must therefore maintain contemporaneous documentation linking expenditures to ongoing technical uncertainties, such as investigating unexpected adverse safety signals, analyzing refractory patient subgroups, modifying dosage formulations to resolve stability or bioavailability failures, or executing adaptive protocol amendments based on interim futility or efficacy analyses.
Qualified Research Expenses (QREs), Statutory Corrections, and Quantitative Reconciliation

Under IRC § 41(b)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a), a taxpayer's Qualified Research Expenses equal the sum of "in-house research expenses" and "contract research expenses" paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer. In the context of clinical trials, QREs fall into three primary operational categories—wages, supplies (alongside narrow off-premises computer use costs), and contract research expenses (CREs)—each governed by strict statutory boundaries and substantiation rules requiring the complete segregation of general and administrative (G&A) overhead.
Statutory Analysis of QRE Categories and Technical Correction on Software Licenses
In-House Wages for Qualified Services (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i))

Qualifying wage expenses encompass compensation, as defined under IRC § 3401(a) subject to federal income tax withholding (or earned income of self-employed individuals under IRC § 401(c)(2), excluding wages taken into account in determining the Work Opportunity Credit under IRC § 51(a)), paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services" performed by such employee within the United States. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c), qualified services are strictly limited to three functional tiers: engaging directly in qualified research, directly supervising qualified research, or directly supporting qualified research.

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(1), "engaging in qualified research" means the actual conduct of qualified research, which in a clinical trial setting encompasses clinical scientists designing trial protocols, biostatisticians developing novel statistical methodologies or patient-stratification algorithms, and clinical trial engineers building prototype biometric capture systems. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2), "direct supervision" means the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research, covering first-line scientific and clinical managers—such as a Clinical Development Director or Medical Monitor—who directly supervise the technical execution of adaptive protocol changes or dose-escalation cohorts; it does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3), "direct support" means services in the direct support of either persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research or persons directly supervising them—such as clinical data managers cleaning and formatting experimental biomarker data streams, laboratory technicians processing trial blood and tissue samples, or clerks compiling research data—while explicitly excluding general administrative services (such as payroll personnel, accountants, janitors, or corporate officers supervising financial or personnel matters) regardless of whether those administrative personnel are assigned to the research department.

Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F), any wages paid for clinical research services performed outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States are strictly excluded. Additionally, under the "substantially all" rule of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2), if an employee devotes at least 80% of their total compensated services during the taxable year to qualified services, 100% of that employee's wages qualify as QREs; otherwise, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1), only the prorated fraction of wages equal to the ratio of total time actually spent performing qualified services to total service time may be claimed.
Supplies Used in the Conduct of Qualified Research (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and § 41(b)(2)(C))

Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), in-house research expenses include amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research. IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) defines "supplies" as any tangible property other than (i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i)–(ii), ordinary utility charges (such as water, electricity, and natural gas) are treated as excluded general and administrative expenses unless the taxpayer establishes that the special character of the qualified research required additional extraordinary expenditures for utilities. In clinical trials, qualifying consumable supplies include chemical reagents, laboratory consumables used in pharmacokinetic and biomarker assays, investigational drug batches synthesized for clinical trial cohorts, disposable wearable sensor modules, and single-use patient-monitoring kits consumed during experimental data collection. Conversely, routine standard-of-care patient medications, patient meals, travel reimbursements, and depreciable laboratory capital equipment do not qualify as supplies.

Under the plain statutory text of IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b), supplies must be tangible personal property; intangible software licenses are not tangible property and therefore cannot be claimed as supply QREs.

For clinical trial software or digital platform expenditures to qualify under IRC § 41(b), they must instead satisfy one of three distinct statutory pathways. First, they may qualify as computer rental or lease costs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4), which cover amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use (time-sharing) computers in the conduct of qualified research, provided the computer is owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer is not the primary user of the computer. Second, if a digital platform vendor is contracted to perform custom software engineering, algorithm validation, or experimental electronic Case Report Form (e-CRF) development on the taxpayer's behalf where the taxpayer bears the financial risk and retains substantial rights, 65% of the service fees may qualify as contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3). Third, wages paid to the taxpayer's own employees developing proprietary clinical trial software or algorithms in-house qualify as internal wage QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) (subject to the high-threshold-of-innovation test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6) if the software is built mainly for the company's own internal back-office use).
Contract Research Expenses (IRC § 41(b)(3))

Under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(1), a taxpayer may claim 65% of any amount paid or incurred to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for qualified research performed on behalf of the taxpayer (or for services which, if performed by employees of the taxpayer, would constitute qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)). In clinical development, payments to Contract Research Organizations (CROs), academic medical centers, research hospitals, independent clinical investigators, and specialized external biostatistics or predictive modeling vendors frequently constitute the largest single category of clinical trial expenditure.

First, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(ii) and (e)(3), the research must be performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer, meaning the taxpayer has a right to the clinical research results (which need not be exclusive, provided the taxpayer retains substantial rights rather than merely receiving an incidental benefit or paying for the right to use the research results). Second, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii), the taxpayer must bear the financial risk (economic risk) of the research, meaning the sponsor is required to bear the expense even if the research is not successful. If an expense is paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement under which payment is contingent on the success of the research, that portion of the payment is considered paid for the product or result rather than the performance of the research and is disqualified as a contract research expense. Additionally, under IRC § 41(b)(3)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(4), if any contract research expense paid or incurred during a taxable year is attributable to qualified research to be conducted after the close of that taxable year, the prepaid amount may only be treated as paid or incurred during the subsequent period in which the qualified research is actually conducted. While IRC § 41(b)(3)(C) allows a 75% inclusion rate for amounts paid to qualified research consortia and IRC § 41(b)(3)(D) allows 100% for eligible energy research payments to universities or federal laboratories (alongside basic research payments under IRC § 41(e)), the standard 65% statutory rate governs commercial CRO and clinical trial vendor contracts.
Hypothetical Worked Examples and Step-by-Step Mathematical Audits
Hypothetical Example 1: Qualitative and Statutory Audit of a Phase IIb Adaptive Dermatology Trial

The trial seeks to resolve technical uncertainty regarding the systemic drug exposure required for clinical efficacy (Criterion 3) by systematically evaluating alternative dosing regimens and delivery methods across adaptive trial arms (Criterion 4). Specifically, the company develops a proprietary patient-stratification algorithm and integrates a remote digital monitoring platform with wearable biometric sensors to adjust dosing protocols in real time.

Applying the verified statutory rules of IRC § 41(b) to this hypothetical scenario requires segregating the expenditures across the three statutory QRE categories. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), salaries paid to the internal U.S.-based biostatistician team for developing and validating the proprietary patient-stratification algorithms qualify at 100% as direct performance of qualified research, and wages paid to the clinical development manager who directly supervises the experimental dosing adjustments in the adaptive trial arms qualify as direct supervision of qualified research. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), the cost of disposable sensor modules and single-use patient-monitoring kits distributed to the 300-patient cohort to capture experimental biomarker data qualifies at 100% as tangible personal property consumed in the conduct of qualified research, provided the hardware is not capitalized as depreciable property. Finally, under IRC § 41(b)(3), fees paid to a third-party CRO to execute a specialized pilot cohort testing two alternative digital data-capture methodologies prior to full trial rollout, as well as contract fees paid to an external analytics vendor for predictive retention modeling on experimental data streams, qualify at the statutory rate of 65%, provided the agreement is entered into prior to performance, the sponsor retains substantial rights, and the sponsor bears the financial risk, while routine site administration and standard patient care expenses such as patient meals or non-experimental hospitality must be segregated and excluded.
Hypothetical Example 2: Mathematical Audit of the BioPharmX Phase II Oncology Study
First, summing the three nominal dollar inputs yields a baseline total of $1,800,000 ($1,200,000 + $450,000 + $150,000 = $1,800,000).

Under Interpretation A, where $1,200,000 represents the gross qualifying CRO expenditure prior to applying the 65% statutory haircut, IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) limits the allowable CRO QRE to 65% of the gross payment, or $780,000 ($1,200,000 × 65% = $780,000). Adding 100% of qualifying internal clinical wages ($450,000) and 100% of qualifying tangible trial supplies ($150,000) yields total statutory QREs of $1,380,000 ($780,000 + $450,000 + $150,000 = $1,380,000). Under Interpretation A, allowable CRO QREs represent 56.52% ($780,000 / $1,380,000), internal wages represent 32.61% ($450,000 / $1,380,000), and trial supplies represent 10.87% ($150,000 / $1,380,000) of the $1,380,000 statutory QRE base. Under Interpretation B, total gross qualifying trial expenditure was $2,446,153.85 ($1,846,153.85 + $450,000 + $150,000), and total statutory QREs equal $1,800,000.

body.text: As a matter of tax law analysis, IRC § 41 provides two statutory calculation methods rather than a flat 10% rate: the Traditional (Regular) Credit under IRC § 41(a)(1), equal to 20% of current-year QREs exceeding a statutory base amount (where the fixed-base percentage is capped at 16% under IRC § 41(c)(3)(C) and the base amount cannot be less than 50% of current-year QREs under IRC § 41(c)(2)), and the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC § 41(c)(4), equal to 14% of current-year QREs exceeding 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years, or 6% of current-year QREs if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years. Furthermore, under IRC § 280C(c)(1)—as amended by Section 70302 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024—a taxpayer's domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A (whether deducted immediately or capitalized) must be reduced by the full amount of the research credit allowed under IRC § 41(a), unless the taxpayer makes an irrevocable election on Item A of Form 6765 (on an original timely filed return, including extensions) under IRC § 280C(c)(2) to claim a reduced credit.

body.text: Compliance Operations and Tax Policy Recommendations
Operational Substantiation Protocols for Clinical Trial Sponsors

Sponsors must systematically archive FDA IND submissions, master clinical trial protocols, protocol amendments, Informed Consent Forms (ICFs), and Institutional Review Board (IRB) correspondence, as these contemporaneous regulatory records establish the specific technical uncertainties present at the outset of each phase and document the systematic process of experimentation used to evaluate alternatives. Simultaneously, enterprise accounting systems must deploy distinct project tracking codes segregated by business component, clinical phase (Phase I, Phase II, Phase III, and Phase IV), and activity type, separating routine "Standard of Care" patient costs and general administrative site management from "Investigational" research costs directly tied to resolving technical uncertainty. Because domestic clinical trial costs are immediately deductible under IRC § 174A(a) and eligible for the IRC § 41 credit while foreign clinical trial costs are excluded from IRC § 41 under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) and subject to 15-year amortization under amended IRC § 174, corporate tax departments must also maintain a strict domestic-versus-foreign split in their general ledgers throughout the year.

Prior to executing clinical trial agreements or work orders with CROs, research hospitals, or external analytics vendors, tax specialists must review contract terms to ensure the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the research, the sponsor explicitly retains substantial rights to the research outputs, the sponsor bears the economic risk of failed experimentation, and vendor invoices segregate U.S.-performed experimental services from foreign trial sites, prepaid future-year research services, and non-qualifying pass-through expenses. Finally, when completing IRS Form 6765, every filer reporting QREs must complete Section E (disclosing the number of business components, officer wages included, and any new expense categories) and, unless exempted via a Qualified Small Business payroll tax election or the small-claim threshold ($1.5 million or less in group-wide QREs and $50 million or less in three-year average gross receipts on an original return), must complete mandatory Section G reporting QREs by discrete business component (identifying wages, supplies, computer costs, and contract research for at least 80% of total QREs, up to 50 business components).
Policy Recommendations and Post-2025 Legislative Status

Because the current non-challenge posture rests on an internal administrative directive (LMSB-04-0404-024) rather than binding regulation, formal codification would insulate early-stage clinical R&D capital planning from shifts in administrative examination policy.

Updated administrative guidance would clearly distinguish qualifying experimental digital infrastructure—such as cloud-based computer leasing costs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(4), tangible disposable biometric sensors under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), and custom engineering vendor contracts under IRC § 41(b)(3)—from routine, general-purpose administrative IT and off-the-shelf software licenses.

With domestic immediate expensing restored under IRC § 174A, ongoing tax planning for clinical trial sponsors now centers on modeling the interaction between IRC § 174A deductions and the IRC § 280C(c)(2) reduced credit election, alongside managing the 15-year amortization and disposition lock-in rules under amended IRC § 174 for foreign clinical trial operations.
